x: How many back-and-forth exchanges a typical user has before the chat ends. Each turn re-sends the earlier history to the model, so later turns cost more than early ones and the total grows faster than the turn count.
y: Support or Q&A chats are often 4 to 10 turns. Check your own logs if you have them.

x: How many times an agent calls the model to finish one task. Every step re-sends the growing context (earlier steps and tool results), so a task with twice the steps costs more than twice as much.
y: Simple agents take 3 to 8 steps. Coding or research agents can take 20 or more.

x: The size of what a tool returns to the model each step: a web page, a search result, a file or a database row. It is added to the context and re-sent on every later step, so large tool results are often the biggest cost in an agent.
y: A search snippet is a few hundred tokens. A full web page or file can be 2,000 to 10,000 or more.

x: What the model writes at each step: a tool call, a short plan or some reasoning. Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens, but agent steps are usually short.
y: 100 to 400 tokens for a tool call or a short plan. Longer if the model reasons out loud.

x: The length of a typical message from your user. It is small compared with the system prompt and the history, so it is rarely what drives the bill.
y: A sentence is about 15 to 25 tokens. A short paragraph is 60 to 100.

x: How much the model writes back per reply. Output is billed at the higher output price, and in a chat each reply is also re-sent as history on later turns, so long replies cost you twice.
y: Chat answers are often 150 to 500 tokens. 750 words is about 1,000 tokens.

x: The standing instructions plus the definitions of the tools the agent can call. Tool definitions count as input and are re-sent with every step, so a large tool list quietly adds cost to every call.
y: Instructions alone are often 500 to 2,000 tokens. Ten or more tools can add several thousand.

x: The fixed instructions sent with every request. Because the model remembers nothing between requests, you pay for them each time, which makes them a good target for trimming and for prompt caching. Paste the text into the box to count it exactly.
y: A short prompt is 200 to 500 tokens. A detailed one with rules and examples is 1,000 to 3,000.

x: The percentage knocked off the price when you run jobs through a provider's batch API, where results come back in hours instead of seconds. Leave it at 0 if you call the normal real-time API.
y: Providers that offer batch pricing commonly discount about 50 percent. Check your provider's current terms.

m: ^conversations per month|^calls per month|^tasks per month
x: How many conversations, calls or tasks you expect in a month. The cost for one is multiplied by this number, so it is the simplest way to scale the estimate from a pilot to production.
y: Start from your real or expected traffic, then try double and ten times to see how the bill scales.

x: How many extra tokens of history each new turn carries forward. None means every turn stands alone. Heavier settings model apps that re-send more of the earlier conversation, which makes input grow with every turn until the context window truncates it.
y: Light is like a short running summary. Heavy is like re-sending most of the chat.

x: When on, the repeated start of your prompt is billed at a discounted cached rate instead of the full input price. It helps most when the same long prompt is sent many times in quick succession, because caches expire after a short time.
y: Turn it on if your system prompt or documents are long and reused. Cached reads are often a fraction of the normal input price.

t: Cached read price (% of input price)
x: What you pay for tokens read from the cache, as a share of the normal input price. Lower means bigger savings. The first time the text is written to the cache some providers charge a little extra, which this estimate does not include.
y: Providers differ, often 10 to 50 percent. Check your provider's current pricing.

x: A cache only stays alive for a few minutes without use. When requests arrive often, most hit a warm cache and cost less. When they are sparse, the cache expires between requests and you pay full price. The chart shows cost per message against how often messages arrive.

As a conversation grows, each request carries more history and costs more. Once the history reaches the model's context window, older content is dropped, so the cost stops rising. The chart shows that curve for your inputs.
Shows how much your monthly cost moves if each input changes by 20 percent up or down. The longest bars are the inputs worth optimizing first, because small changes there move the bill the most.
Drag a slider to change an input and watch the monthly cost respond, without editing the main form. Use it to test ideas such as a shorter system prompt or fewer turns.
Splits the monthly cost into its parts: normal input, cached input (if caching is on) and output. The biggest part shows where the money goes.
What it would cost to send this exact text to each model once as input, using the model's input price. Output tokens are not included, because the reply depends on the model and your prompt.

m: ^how will you use this text|^how is this prompt used
x: Decides how often the text is sent. A batch prompt is sent once per call. A chatbot system prompt is re-sent on every turn and an agent's on every step, so the same text costs more in the later cases. The monthly estimates use this.

Each model family splits text into tokens in its own way. OpenAI publishes its tokenizers, so those counts are exact. For Claude, Gemini and others the tool gives an estimate, usually within 10 to 15 percent, which is fine for budgeting but not for hitting a hard limit.
The size of each piece when a long document is split. Small chunks match questions more precisely but lose surrounding context. Large chunks keep context but are less targeted and cost more to send.
y: For search over documents, 200 to 800 tokens is a common starting point.

x: How many tokens are repeated at the end of one chunk and the start of the next. Overlap stops an idea that falls on a boundary from being cut in half, at the cost of some duplicated tokens.
y: About 10 to 20 percent of the chunk size is typical.

x: Type a question you expect users to ask and the tool shows which chunks match it best, using keyword matching. If the right chunk does not appear, your chunk size or overlap may need adjusting.
Write the fixed instructions once and put the changing details in double curly braces, like {{topic}}. When you use the template you fill in each variable, so every prompt has the same structure.

A description of the shape the JSON must have: required fields, their types and allowed values. Paste one and the validator reports exactly what a model's output got wrong, such as a missing field or a number returned as text.
What the provider charges for every million tokens you send to the model. To estimate a request, multiply your input tokens by this price and divide by a million.
What the provider charges for every million tokens the model writes. It is usually several times the input price, so long answers are the expensive part.
Hides models whose input price per million tokens is above this number. Use it to see only the models that fit your budget.
The most text the model can handle in a single request, in thousands of tokens. Your prompt, history and the reply all have to fit inside it.
y: About 750 words per 1K tokens, so 128K is roughly a 300-page book.

x: How many times more the model charges for output than for input. A high ratio hurts workloads that write long answers. A low ratio suits ones that write a lot.
Whether your input tokens plus the reply fit inside the model's context window. If not, the request would fail or be truncated.

Your input tokens times the input price, plus your output tokens times the output price, divided by a million. Per month multiplies by your requests per month. The comparison shows each model against the cheapest one.
The company that hosts the model and sets its price. The same underlying model can be sold by several providers at different prices.
The largest request, in tokens, that the model accepts. The ranking shows which models can handle your text in one go.
Chooses which model's price and context window the estimate uses. Prices differ by a large factor between small and large models, so try a few.
